newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Black sticks nose in last white S.African bastion.
newsitem.headline: Black sticks nose in last white S.African bastion.

text.p: Twenty years ago, Jabulani Ntshangase might have seen a wine bottle as a potential Molotov cocktail in the fight against apartheid.
Today he would reverently sniff the bouquet, taste a mouthful and pronounce on the ripeness of the wine's tannins, the fullness of its body or the persistence of its tail.
Ntshangase, who went into exile in 1977, returned to South Africa last year as its first black wine connoisseur.

Now he is collaborating with insurance tycoon Dick Enthoven in an ambitious project based at the Spier wine estate near Stellenbosch to spread the profits and pleasures of the vine to South Africa's black majority.
"The history of wine in South Africa is predominantly white. The vineyards and cellars have been owned by whites," Ntshangase said in an interview.

"Now I'm trying to bring a balance. When we talk about wine tasting, every time we take a look at the wine, every time we take a sniff at the wine, we're looking for a balance, and that's what we're looking to get in the industry, to have a balance."
Enthoven, who spent several years in South Africa's whites- only parliament as a liberal opponent of apartheid, bought Spier in 1993 and hired Ntshangase as his "wine ambassador".
"Jabulani was hired for his passion for wine, his knowledge and understanding," he said. "We perceive ourselves as the quintessential wine experience in South Africa and he is fundamental to that."
GRAPES OF EMPOWERMENT
Endtoven has set up a development trust which he foresees becoming a player in black empowerment, the process of selling slices of white-owned assets to black capitalists.
"We eventually envisage Spier plus a lot of the businesses that will be part of it becoming a public company," he said.
"Then this Spier Development Trust will get substantial options and hopefully will be able to exercise those options to become part of the controlling consortium of Spier."
Apart from helping blacks to get rich out of wine, the trust is seeking to encourage them to learn to appreciate what has until now been an almost exclusively white drink in South Africa.
The trust is training black wine merchants and is paying for three or four blacks to study wine-making at Stellenbosch University.

One of South Africa's leading wine merchants, Vaughan Johnson, said it was only a matter of time before the country's 35 million blacks -- nearly 90 percent of the population -- began drinking more wine.
"If you look at the former colonies north of South Africa, those which had Portuguese or French landlords, their people have all become great wine drinkers," he said.

South African wine exports have increased ten-fold -- to 10 million cases this year -- since 1990, when the process of scrapping apartheid began and it became acceptable for foreigners to drink the country's wines.
EMERGING FROM THE "DARK AGES"

Ntshangase said the years of apartheid isolation had taken their toll on the quality of South African wine, which is often compared unfavourably with that of the country's main export competitors, Australia and California.
"The wine industry suffered during those dark ages," he said. "There's a lot of work to be done."

Ntshangase left South Africa as a teetotaller after the widespread student riots of 1976, studying embalming in Britain before ending up in a New York City wine store where he unloaded trucks, packed shelves, and began his wine apprenticeship.
Now when he meets fellow wine experts in South Africa, "they just are amazed".
"People think I cannot be South African," Ntshangase said.
He praised Enthoven for his willingness to bring black trainees into Spier, which is being transformed from a run-down wine producer into a tourist hub for South Africa's winelands.
A steam train runs from Cape Town to Spier's private railway station, three hotels with up to 600 beds are planned, and an amphitheatre provides the stage for music and theatre.

"At this stage it's all self-funded but once the hotel goes up I think we will be doing some gearing," Enthoven said, adding that "the big vision" for Spier depended on the current boom in foreign tourism continuing.
